title: Ten pounds (Luke 19:11–27)
hook: Luke's version of the talents: be faithful with a little

segments.voice: Yesterday, salvation came to this house, and Zacchaeus paid back fourfold. Your line was today, salvation. What did you repay? Day five hundred sixty-nine.

Luke says Jesus is now nigh to Jerusalem, and he tells us exactly what's in the air: "they thought that the kingdom of God should immediately appear." Any day now. Maybe tomorrow. Jesus is heading into the capital, a healer and teacher with a crowd behind him, and people are ready for a coronation. So he tells them a story about a coronation that takes a long time to arrive, and about what to do in the meantime, with very little in your hands.

A nobleman goes to a far country to receive a kingdom and then return. Some scholars think Jesus' listeners would have recognized that: the historian Josephus tells how, after Herod the Great died, his son Archelaus traveled to Rome to have his rule confirmed, and a delegation went after him to protest. In the story, too, the citizens send word: "We will not have this man to reign over us." Before he leaves, he calls ten servants and gives each of them one pound. In Greek, a mina: a real sum of money, but small next to a kingdom. And here's the big difference from Matthew's parable of the talents. There, servants get different amounts. Here, everyone gets exactly the same. His instruction in the King James Bible is "Occupy till I come." Occupy means do business, put it to work. When he returns, the first servant says: "Lord, thy pound hath gained ten pounds." And the answer: "Well, thou good servant: because thou hast been faithful in a very little, have thou authority over ten cities." A very little. Ten cities. The reward is wildly out of proportion to the test. Another made five. Then one comes and says: "Lord, behold, here is thy pound, which I have kept laid up in a napkin." Wrapped in a cloth, safe and useless, because he was afraid. Christians read this parable in more than one way. The traditional reading hears the nobleman as Christ, gone away and coming back, asking what his people did with what they were given. Some modern readers notice how harsh the nobleman is and hear a warning about earthly kings instead. Either way, the servants' question is ours: what do you do with a very little, while you wait?
screen: then, large: `FAITHFUL IN A VERY LITTLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: invest one small gift. Settle and breathe. Think of one small thing you have that you've been keeping wrapped up. A skill you don't use much, a little spare time, a modest amount of money, a talent for listening, cooking, fixing things, making people laugh. Nothing grand, just one pound. Notice what's kept it in the napkin: fear of getting it wrong, a sense that it's too small to matter. Now picture putting it to work this week, for someone else. One concrete step. If you pray, you can offer it back to God. The bell holds the time.
Ten pounds. Ten servants each given the same single pound, told to put it to work until their master returns, and rewarded for being faithful in a very little.
Your line: faithful in a very little. Today, take your one small gift out of the napkin and use it once. Day five hundred sixty-nine.

howItsDone: In Christian teaching, gifts and talents are often described as given by God to be used for others, and churches encourage people to discover and use their gifts in service, in the congregation and beyond.

original.note: Greek: a mina, a sum of money. the King James Bible says pound.

trapdoor: what you thought: the same story as the talents.
what it means: everyone gets the same small gift, and the question is what you do with a very little while you wait.
what a scholar hears: the nobleman's journey echoes Archelaus going to Rome to claim his throne, and readers differ on whether the harsh nobleman stands for Christ or a warning about earthly kings.

notes: Archelaus's journey to Rome and the protesting delegation (Josephus, Antiquities 17; Jewish War 2): confirm reference.
Mina ≈ 100 drachmas ≈ about 100 days' wages: confirm.
The harsh ending (19:27) is not quoted; the two readings (nobleman as Christ vs critique of earthly kings) are presented without ranking.
Ten servants are given pounds, but only three report; not mentioned to keep one idea.
